reference.quote: Booking.com does not authorize the use of automated means or automated assistants (including... AI-powered assistants) to make bookings or reservations using anything on our Platform without the prior, express written permission of Booking.com

exposures.title: Every visit is watched, and too many searches gets you blocked
exposures.whatItMeans: Booking.com states it keeps a close eye on every visit to the platform and will block anyone, or any automated system, it suspects of conducting an unreasonable amount of searches, using any device or software to gather prices or other information, placing undue stress on the platform, or using AI assistants without permission.
exposures.whyItMatters: No threshold is published for what counts as unreasonable, and comparison shopping across dates and properties is exactly what a traveller does. Being blocked from a platform mid-trip is a real cost attached to an undefined limit.

reference.label: Intellectual property rights
reference.quote: We keep a close eye on every visit to our Platform, and we'll block anyone (and any automated system) we suspect of

exposures.title: A cancelled booking may cost you the money and the explanation
exposures.whatItMeans: Breaching the terms, the values, or the content guidelines, or failing to comply with applicable law, lets Booking.com stop you booking, cancel bookings you have already made, and cut off your account and access to customer service. If it cancels on that basis you may not be entitled to a refund, and it may decline to tell you why where doing so would contravene law or obstruct fraud detection.
exposures.whyItMatters: The trigger includes 'our values', which are stated as broad conduct expectations rather than specific rules — not causing a nuisance, behaving appropriately. A cancelled trip with no refund and no stated reason leaves nothing to contest beyond a customer-service request.

exposures.title: Outside Europe you must sue in Amsterdam or England, wherever you live
exposures.whatItMeans: Consumers living in the EEA, UK or Switzerland may bring an action in the courts of their own country, and Booking.com may only sue them there. For consumers outside Europe, to the extent local mandatory consumer law permits, any dispute is submitted exclusively to the court in Amsterdam or in England and Wales depending on what was booked.
exposures.whyItMatters: The same booking, the same company, and the practical availability of a court decided by where the traveller lives. The mandatory-local-law qualifier is a genuine safeguard, but it puts the burden on a consumer in Delhi or São Paulo to establish that their own law overrides the clause.

exposures.title: The provider can cancel without notice if the balance does not clear, and refund at its discretion
exposures.whatItMeans: Where you pay in advance, the service provider may cancel the booking without notice if it cannot collect the balance on the specified date, and any non-refundable payment already made is refunded only at the provider's discretion. Making sure the payment goes through is stated to be your responsibility.
exposures.whyItMatters: A card that expires or a bank that declines a foreign charge is enough to lose both the reservation and the deposit, with no notice step that would let the traveller fix it and no right to the money back.

exposures.title: Genius status and earned rewards can be withdrawn or restructured
exposures.whatItMeans: Booking.com may change any feature of the Genius programme including membership levels, which booking types count toward progression, and how the programme is structured. Where it investigates fraud, misuse or abuse it may cancel a membership and the rewards already earned. Rewards are issued at its sole discretion, and it may correct balances for clerical errors.
exposures.whyItMatters: Genius levels are earned by completing a set number of bookings over two years — an investment of real spending against a benefit whose terms and thresholds can be changed after the spending is done.

exposures.title: Your review photo can be used commercially anywhere, until you ask it to stop
exposures.whatItMeans: Uploading a review or picture confirms Booking.com may use it on the platform and for any other commercial purpose including marketing and advertising, on any media, worldwide — unless you ask it to stop. You also accept full responsibility for any legal claim against Booking.com relating to it.
exposures.whyItMatters: The licence is broad, but it is revocable on request, which is rare. Almost every comparable clause in this corpus is perpetual and irrevocable, so the notable thing here is what the drafters did not take.

reference.label: Intellectual property rights
reference.quote: we're allowed to use it on our Platform and for any other commercial purposes (including marketing and advertising), on any media, worldwide—unless you ask us to stop using it

exposures.title: You carry the whole group's behaviour and their data consent
exposures.whatItMeans: As the person making the booking you are responsible for the actions and behaviour of everyone in the group in relation to the travel experience, and for obtaining their permission before providing Booking.com with their personal data.
exposures.whyItMatters: Group misconduct can trigger the cancellation and no-refund provisions above, and the person on the hook is whoever held the card. The data-permission duty is transferred to a traveller with no way to evidence it.

exposures.title: The conditions you see may be part of an experiment
exposures.whatItMeans: Booking.com states it shows different people different designs, phrasings and products to find out how they react, and that as a result you might not come across some services or conditions when you visit the platform.
exposures.whyItMatters: Naming 'conditions' alongside designs and phrasings means the terms attached to an offer, not only its presentation, may vary between users at the same moment. Disclosing this is more than most peers do; it also means what you were shown is not necessarily what was available.

availableActions.action: Rely on your own consumer law — the terms say it wins
availableActions.howTo: Booking.com states plainly that mandatory consumer protection laws guarantee rights no company's terms can overrule, and that where they conflict, those laws override. It is the clearest such statement in this corpus; quote it when a clause is used against you.

reference.label: Limitation of liability
reference.quote: If there is any inconsistency between those laws and regulations and these Terms, such mandatory consumer protection laws and regulations will override.

availableActions.action: European consumers: sue at home
availableActions.howTo: If you live in the EEA, UK or Switzerland you may bring an action in the courts of your own country as well as in Amsterdam or England and Wales, and Booking.com may only sue you in your home courts. You can also rely on your national consumer law.

availableActions.action: Escalate a complaint to a named regulator
availableActions.howTo: Complaints go first to Customer Service — by post to Postbus 1639, 1000 BP Netherlands, through the Help Center, or by phone — with your booking confirmation number, reservation PIN and supporting documents; all complaints are recorded trackably. Czech residents can escalate to the Czech Trade Inspection Authority's ADR department at adr@coi.cz; Brazilian residents to consumidor.gov.br. Note the EU ODR platform stopped accepting new claims on 20 March 2025.

availableActions.action: EU users: challenge a content action through an out-of-court provider
availableActions.howTo: If Booking.com applies content actions to your content or account and you are in the EU, you may raise a dispute with a certified out-of-court dispute settlement provider from its published list. Their decisions are not binding on Booking.com, but the route exists and costs less than litigation.

availableActions.action: Ask Booking.com to stop using a photo you uploaded
availableActions.howTo: The commercial licence over review pictures is expressly subject to you asking it to stop. Almost no comparable clause in this corpus is revocable — send the request rather than assuming the grant is permanent.

availableActions.action: Book before a terms change if you want the current terms
availableActions.howTo: Material changes are notified in advance, and existing bookings continue to be governed by the terms that applied when the booking was made. Changes are not retroactive, which is worth knowing when a notice arrives mid-trip.

availableActions.action: Keep the card that will be charged for the balance alive
availableActions.howTo: Where the balance is collected later, a failed collection lets the provider cancel without notice and refund any advance payment only at its discretion. Check the expiry date and available funds against the collection date shown in the booking.

availableActions.action: Choose the provider's currency, not 'Pay In Your Own Currency'
availableActions.howTo: Booking.com offers conversion into your home currency as principal rather than as agent for the provider, under separate terms that give you no extra rights under your booking contract. Paying in the provider's currency keeps the conversion — and any dispute about the rate — with your own bank.

availableActions.action: France: register on Bloctel
availableActions.howTo: The terms point French users who have given a phone number to the national do-not-call list at www.bloctel.gouv.fr. It is the only country-specific marketing opt-out named in the document.

availableActions.action: Read the provider's cancellation and no-show policy, not these terms
availableActions.howTo: Cancellation fees, no-show fees and refunds all follow the service provider's policy shown during booking, in the fine print and in the confirmation. Some bookings cannot be cancelled free at all; others only before a deadline.

requiredDisclosures.name: Consumer rights preservation
requiredDisclosures.note: Stated twice over: liability is not limited for death or personal injury from negligence, fraud, gross negligence or wilful misconduct, or anything not lawfully excludable — and mandatory consumer protection law expressly overrides the terms where they conflict. The strongest such statement in the corpus.

requiredDisclosures.name: Notice of changes to terms
requiredDisclosures.note: Advance notice before material changes take effect, unless the change is required by law, with continued use after the effective date constituting acceptance.

requiredDisclosures.name: Non-retroactivity of changes
requiredDisclosures.note: Existing bookings continue to be governed by the terms that applied when the booking was made. Only LinkedIn's user agreement makes a comparable commitment.

requiredDisclosures.name: Governing law and jurisdiction
requiredDisclosures.note: Dutch law for accommodation, flights and attractions; English law for car rentals and ground transport. European consumers may sue at home or in Amsterdam or England and Wales, and may only be sued at home. Non-European consumers get exclusive Amsterdam or England and Wales jurisdiction, subject to mandatory local consumer law. No arbitration clause and no class-action waiver.

requiredDisclosures.name: Consumer complaint route
requiredDisclosures.note: Postal address, Help Center, phone and messaging, with complaints recorded in an identifiable trackable way. Named escalation routes for the EEA (ODR, with its 20 March 2025 discontinuation disclosed), Czechia and Brazil, plus EU out-of-court dispute settlement providers for content actions.

requiredDisclosures.name: Refund and cancellation rights
requiredDisclosures.note: Deferred to each provider's cancellation and no-show policy, displayed during booking and in the confirmation, with free-cancellation deadlines flagged. Obvious pricing errors are not binding but are refunded.

requiredDisclosures.name: Automatic renewal disclosure
requiredDisclosures.note: No subscription product. Genius membership is free and carries no recurring charge; rewards and credits are issued at Booking.com's discretion.

requiredDisclosures.name: Named Grievance Officer
requiredDisclosures.note: A Netherlands and UK-governed document with no India-facing entity; the IT Rules grievance-officer requirement does not attach. Regulator escalation routes are named for the jurisdictions the document does cover.

analyses.summary: The best-drafted payments privacy policy in this corpus — a named Data Protection Officer, a Nodal and Grievance Officer for India, per-country sections for a dozen jurisdictions, escalation routes to actual regulators, and an express promise that refusing to give your Aadhaar will not get you refused service. What it discloses is still wide. Abandoning a checkout does not stop your data reaching the merchant, who may then market to you. Stripe's Financial Connections periodically collects your bank balances and transactions and, in some cases, your log-in credentials. Mouse-movement patterns are collected as a fraud signal and personal data trains AI models with no opt-out described. Most people covered by this policy are 'End Customers' whose data Stripe holds as a processor — which means their rights must be exercised against the merchant, and if Stripe cannot identify that merchant, there is nowhere to go. No retention period is stated anywhere except a one-year biometric limit that applies only in New Zealand.

exposures.title: Abandoning the checkout still sends your details to the merchant, who may market to you
exposures.whatItMeans: Stripe may collect information entered into a checkout form even where you choose not to complete the form or the transaction. If you started a purchase, the business receives your personal data from Stripe whether or not you finished, and may use it to market and advertise its products subject to its own privacy policy.
exposures.whyItMatters: Closing the tab is how people decline a transaction, and this makes the decision to decline the moment the data transfers. Whatever rights you then have run against the merchant's policy, not Stripe's.

reference.label: Advertising by Business Users
reference.quote: the Business User receives your Personal Data from us in connection with our provision of Services even if you don't finish your purchase

exposures.title: Financial Connections collects your balances, transactions and sometimes your log-in credentials
exposures.whatItMeans: Linking a bank account through Stripe's Financial Connections means Stripe periodically collects and processes account owner information, balances, account number and details, transactions and, in some cases, log-in credentials. Consent is withdrawn by disconnecting the account.
exposures.whyItMatters: Periodic means it continues after the transaction that prompted it. Log-in credentials are the category that would let someone act as you at your bank, and the qualifier 'in some cases' does not say which.

reference.label: Using Link or Connecting your bank account
reference.quote: Stripe will periodically collect and process your account information (such as bank account owner information, account balances, account number and details, account transactions, and, in some cases, log-in credentials)

exposures.title: Most people this policy covers cannot exercise their rights against Stripe at all
exposures.whatItMeans: When you buy from a business using Stripe you are an 'End Customer', and Stripe processes your data as a processor on that business's instructions. To exercise data rights you must approach the business. If you contact Stripe, it will refer you to the controller 'to the extent we are able to identify them'.
exposures.whyItMatters: That qualifier is the exposure. Anyone who paid through a Stripe checkout and cannot now name the merchant — a one-off purchase, a business that has since closed — has data held by a company that says it may not be able to route the request anywhere.

reference.label: Process for exercising your data protection rights
reference.quote: we will refer you to the relevant data controller to the extent we are able to identify them

exposures.title: In India, staying silent counts as consenting
exposures.whatItMeans: Under the India section, Stripe states it may rely on 'legitimate use' under Section 7 of the DPDPA, giving as its first example that where you voluntarily provide personal data without indicating that you do not consent to its use, you will be deemed to have given consent. Acceptance of the policy is separately characterised as a clear affirmative action.
exposures.whyItMatters: This converts India's consent regime into an opt-out at the moment of handing over data, and there is no described way to indicate non-consent while still completing the transaction. Singapore's section relies on the equivalent 'deemed consent' route.

reference.label: India
reference.quote: When you voluntarily provide your Personal Data to us without indicating that you do not consent to its use, you will be deemed to have given your consent.

exposures.title: No retention period, and retention continues past the end of the relationship
exposures.whatItMeans: Data is kept for as long as Stripe provides services to you or a business you dealt with, or for a period in which it reasonably foresees continuing to do so — and after you close your account or complete a transaction, for legal and regulatory obligations, fraud monitoring, and tax and accounting requirements including those set by contract with its financial partners.
exposures.whyItMatters: 'A period in which we reasonably foresee continuing to provide the Services' is a forecast, not a limit. The only actual figure in the whole document is a one-year cap on biometric data, and it appears in the New Zealand section only, so it applies to New Zealanders alone.

exposures.title: Your personal data trains Stripe's AI models, with no opt-out
exposures.whatItMeans: Training artificial intelligence models to power the services and protect against fraud is listed among the ways Stripe analyses, improves and develops its services, using personal data collected across End Users, End Customers, Representatives and Visitors. Call recordings and chat transcripts are separately analysed for quality assurance, training and operational purposes.
exposures.whyItMatters: No opt-out, objection route or exclusion is described for model training, in a document that otherwise names a specific control for almost everything else — biometric verification, bank connections, marketing, Aadhaar.

reference.label: Analyzing, Improving, and Developing our Services

exposures.title: Under US financial privacy law most sharing cannot be limited, and it outlives the relationship
exposures.whatItMeans: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley notice shows Stripe shares for everyday business purposes, its own marketing and joint marketing with other financial companies, with no ability to limit any of them. The categories shared include Social Security number, account balances, transaction history and credit reports. The notice states that sharing continues when you are no longer a customer.
exposures.whyItMatters: The same structure as PayPal's notice: the only limitable categories are the three federal law compels, and everything else is outside the customer's control by design. Ending the relationship does not end the sharing.

reference.label: US Consumer Privacy Notice
reference.quote: When you are no longer our customer, we continue to share your information as described in this notice.

exposures.title: How you move your mouse is a fraud signal Stripe collects
exposures.whatItMeans: Alongside IP address, plug-ins, language preference, time spent, pages visited, links clicked and payment methods used across Stripe's own sites and third-party sites, Stripe collects activity indicators such as mouse activity indicators to help detect fraud.
exposures.whyItMatters: Pointer dynamics are a behavioural signal that can distinguish one person from another across sessions, and because Stripe's checkout is embedded on other companies' sites, the collection happens on pages the user does not associate with Stripe.

reference.label: Online Activity
reference.quote: We also collect activity indicators, such as mouse activity indicators, to help us detect fraud.

exposures.title: Applying for a card through a Stripe-powered business pulls a credit report
exposures.whatItMeans: For consumer credit cards issued through Stripe Issuing, Stripe collects your name, address, email, identity documents, tax ID and self-reported income, and may obtain credit reports from credit bureaus to determine eligibility. It also collects transaction data from the card's use. Separately, Stripe conducts credit checks where lawfully permitted as part of fraud prevention.
exposures.whyItMatters: The card carries the brand of the business you know, so the credit inquiry and the resulting file sit with an infrastructure company most cardholders have no relationship with and would not think to query.

exposures.title: A buyer of Stripe's business gets to keep using your data
exposures.whatItMeans: In a reorganisation, merger, sale, joint venture, assignment, transfer or change of control, personal data may be shared with third parties, and any entity that buys Stripe or part of its business has the right to continue using your data subject to this policy.
exposures.whyItMatters: The protection carried across is this policy, which the acquirer may then change under its own update clause. For an infrastructure provider holding transaction histories for a large share of online commerce, the identity of the holder is part of the risk.

availableActions.action: India: refuse Aadhaar — the policy says you will not be denied service
availableActions.howTo: Providing Aadhaar to a third-party verification partner is stated to be purely voluntary, other identification documents are accepted, and Stripe commits that you will not be denied service for withholding it. This is a stronger and more explicit commitment than any comparable clause in the corpus.

reference.label: India
reference.quote: You will not be denied service merely for not submitting Aadhaar details.

availableActions.action: Disconnect a linked bank account to stop ongoing collection
availableActions.howTo: Financial Connections collects account data periodically, not once. The policy states you can withdraw consent by disconnecting the bank account and ask Stripe to cease collection at any time — which is the only way to stop the recurring pull.

reference.label: Using Link or Connecting your bank account

availableActions.action: Revoke biometric verification consent separately
availableActions.howTo: Using your biometric data to enhance Stripe's verification technology is a separate consent from the identity check itself, and can be revoked at any time. In New Zealand the biometric data from Stripe Identity is retained for one year and alternative verification options are documented.

availableActions.action: Appeal a refused request to the DPO, then to a regulator
availableActions.howTo: Stripe states a right to appeal any decision about your rights by contacting the Data Protection Officer at dpo@stripe.com — Adi Gilad is named in the Brazil section — and to go to regulators: the Irish Data Protection Commission for the EEA, the UK ICO, the Data Protection Board of India, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, the New Zealand Privacy Commissioner. Unresolved concerns under the Data Privacy Framework go free of charge to TrustArc's watchdog form.

availableActions.action: India: use the Nodal and Grievance Officer, in your own language
availableActions.howTo: The India section names a Nodal and Grievance Officer for questions and complaints, and offers to provide the policy or communicate about privacy in one of India's official languages. Escalation runs to the Data Protection Board of India if Stripe cannot resolve the grievance.

availableActions.action: Ask for the list of third parties your data went to
availableActions.howTo: Stripe recognises a right to confirmation of the categories of personal data processed and of the third parties or categories of third parties it is shared with. Brazilian residents have a specific LGPD right to obtain information about the public or private entities Stripe has shared their data with.

availableActions.action: India: nominate someone to exercise your rights if you die or lose capacity
availableActions.howTo: The DPDPA section gives a right to nominate another individual who may exercise your rights in the event of your death or incapacity. Almost no other document in this corpus offers a succession route for data rights.

availableActions.action: End Customers: go to the merchant, and keep the receipt that names them
availableActions.howTo: For data Stripe holds as a processor, rights are exercised against the business you bought from, not Stripe. Stripe will only refer you onward to the extent it can identify the controller — so the transaction record identifying the merchant is what makes the right usable at all.

reference.label: Process for exercising your data protection rights

availableActions.action: Unsubscribe from marketing, and expect merchant messages to continue
availableActions.howTo: The unsubscribe link stops Stripe's marketing. Service, support and legal notices continue, and the policy states that businesses you deal with may still send you messages or instruct Stripe to send them on their behalf — those have to be stopped with the merchant.

reference.label: Opting out of receiving electronic communications from us

availableActions.action: Assume calls are recorded and transcribed
availableActions.howTo: Calls with Stripe or its representatives may be recorded and transcribed where permitted by law, and recordings and chat transcripts are analysed for quality assurance, training and operational purposes.

requiredDisclosures.name: Retention period
requiredDisclosures.note: Criteria only, extended by a forecast of continuing to provide services. The single figure in the entire document is one year for biometric data, stated in the New Zealand section under the Biometric Privacy Processing Code and applying only there.

requiredDisclosures.name: Data protection officer contact
requiredDisclosures.note: dpo@stripe.com throughout, with the DPO named as Adi Gilad in the Brazil section and a separately identified Global Head of Privacy at privacy@stripe.com for Canada and Quebec.

requiredDisclosures.name: Named Grievance Officer
requiredDisclosures.note: A Nodal and Grievance Officer is designated for India with an escalation route to the Data Protection Board of India, and an offer to communicate about privacy in an official Indian language — though the officer is identified behind a link rather than named inline.

requiredDisclosures.name: International transfer safeguards
requiredDisclosures.note: The most thorough in the corpus: adequacy decisions, EU Standard Contractual Clauses with the UK IDTA Addendum and a Brazilian variant, EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework certification with the UK Extension, APEC CBPR and PRP certifications, Japanese APPI equivalent-measure agreements, and free third-party dispute resolution through TrustArc.

requiredDisclosures.name: GLBA consumer privacy notice
requiredDisclosures.note: Full model-form notice with the sharing table, the categories shared including Social Security number and credit reports, and the statement that sharing continues after you cease to be a customer. Everyday business, own marketing and joint marketing are all non-limitable.

requiredDisclosures.name: AI training opt-out
requiredDisclosures.note: Training AI models is disclosed as a use of personal data across all four data-subject categories, with no opt-out, objection route or exclusion described — the one significant processing purpose in the document with no attached control.

requiredDisclosures.name: Automated decision-making rights
requiredDisclosures.note: Committed in the Australia section: where automated decisions could reasonably be expected to significantly affect rights or interests, Stripe will provide the legally required information and transparency, via the Privacy Center or case by case.

requiredDisclosures.name: Lawful basis for processing
requiredDisclosures.note: A dedicated section, with jurisdiction-specific bases named — DPDPA Section 7 legitimate use in India, deemed consent in Singapore, public interest under the APPI in Japan — though the detail is deferred to the linked Privacy Center rather than set out in the policy itself.

requiredDisclosures.name: Children's data
requiredDisclosures.note: Services are not directed to children under 13, with a request that they not provide personal data, and higher age limits imposed where local law requires.

requiredDisclosures.name: Notice of changes to terms
requiredDisclosures.note: A 'Last updated' legend marks material revisions, changes are effective on the later of posting or any notice the law requires, and End Users and Representatives may additionally be contacted through the Stripe Dashboard, email or the postal address on the account.
